fixability.reason: additive index, zero behaviour risk (payment_allocation is read on allocated_amount and no existing index leads with that column)

ranked.claim: Hibernate’s hydration of each result row into a CollectionsRowDto adds ~0.08 ms per row (~8 ms per request).

fixability.reason: DTO projection returns the same values (customer_payment: 3 of 6 columns are read)

ranked.claim: Serializing the DTO list to JSON consumes ~0.05 ms per row (~5 ms per request).

candidates.description: Create a composite index on customer_payment(method, paid_on) to let MySQL use the index for the method equality and paid_on range predicates, eliminating the full table scan on CustomerPayment.
candidates.sql_change: CREATE INDEX idx_customer_payment_method_paid_on ON customer_payment (method, paid_on);
what_could_break: If the index creation takes a long time it could lock the table during migration.
If the query planner chooses a sub‑optimal plan despite the index, rows examined may not drop as expected.
candidates.not_selectable_because:
this patch changes the database schema, and both arms resolve to the SAME schema: mysql://localhost:3307/mini.
An index is a property of the database, not of a worktree. Once green's migration applies it, blue is querying an indexed table too, so an interleaved A/B would compare two arms that both have the index and report no improvement for a change that may be worth a great deal. That is a false negative, and it looks exactly like the system working.
The measurement was NOT run. This is not a statement that the patch does not help — it is a statement that this harness cannot currently find out. Give each arm its own schema and run again; docs/schema-changes.md says what that requires.

candidates.description: Rewrite the JPQL‑generated SQL to avoid the FUNCTION('DATE', …) call and compare the timestamp column directly, allowing the new (method, paid_on) index to be used.
candidates.sql_before: SELECT c.name, i.id, cp.paid_on, pa.allocated_amount FROM payment_allocation pa JOIN customer_payment cp ON pa.payment_id = cp.id JOIN invoice i ON pa.invoice_id = i.id JOIN customer c ON i.customer_id = c.id WHERE DATE(cp.paid_on) >= %s AND DATE(cp.paid_on) < %s AND cp.method = %s ORDER BY cp.paid_on ASC, cp.id ASC, pa.id ASC LIMIT %s OFFSET %s
candidates.sql_after: SELECT c.name, i.id, cp.paid_on, pa.allocated_amount FROM payment_allocation pa JOIN customer_payment cp ON pa.payment_id = cp.id JOIN invoice i ON pa.invoice_id = i.id JOIN customer c ON i.customer_id = c.id WHERE cp.paid_on >= %s AND cp.paid_on < %s AND cp.method = %s ORDER BY cp.paid_on ASC, cp.id ASC, pa.id ASC LIMIT %s OFFSET %s
what_could_break: Changing the WHERE clause semantics could alter results if time components are present; however the original query truncates to date, and the new range comparison is equivalent for the given date‑only parameters.
